item.title: AWS Simplifies WAF Pricing with Three-Dimensional Model
item.description:
AWS Simplifies WAF Pricing with Three-Dimensional Model

📊 Overview

Starting today, AWS WAF pricing is easier to predict. Your bill is now based on three dimensions: the resources you protect, the traffic AWS WAF inspects, and the level of protection you apply to that traffic. For new or smaller workloads, the Free plan of CloudFront flat-rate pricing plans is another way to start. If your application serves fewer than 1 million requests per month, the Free plan costs $0 per month for each CloudFront distribution. It includes AWS WAF protection against common web threats, DDoS protection, and the CloudFront CDN, with no overage charges.

⚙️ Key Details

  • Adding a protection (such as a rule, Bot Control, or Anti-DDoS rule group) no longer adds a subscription or a separate per-request charge. Those requests bill at the base request rate.
  • Capacity no longer affects your rate. Each protection pack (web ACL) now includes up to 2,500 web ACL capacity units (WCUs), up from 1,500, and going past your included capacity does not raise what you pay per request.
  • The premium request fee applies only to the traffic you choose to send through advanced protections.
  • You can estimate costs before writing a first rule, and those estimates hold even as your rules change.
  • Security rules change often. Adding, reordering, or removing rules does not change your rate.
  • For AWS Shield Advanced subscribers, nothing changes. Your Shield Advanced subscription, its price, and your included AWS WAF entitlement stay the same.
  • Customers on a CloudFront flat-rate pricing plan also see no change.

💰 How Costs Are Calculated

AWS WAF bills three fees:

Fee Type Description
Resource Fee Hourly charge for each resource associated with a protection pack (e.g., CloudFront distributions, Application Load Balancers, Amazon API Gateway APIs).
Base Request Fee Applies to each request AWS WAF inspects.
Premium Request Fee Applies on top of the base request fee, to requests evaluated by advanced protections like Bot Control, Fraud Control, API Security, and AI Security.

Both API Security and AI Security use the same premium request fee, with no separate subscription or rate. Requests evaluated by one or more advanced protections are billed $5.60 per million: the $0.60 base request fee plus the $5.00 premium request fee. AWS WAF charges the premium request fee once per request, however many advanced protections evaluate it. A request blocked before reaching an advanced protection pays only the base request fee.

🚀 Availability and Transition

  • Existing AWS WAF customers move to the new pricing on February 1, 2027. Until then, they keep their current pricing and don’t need to do anything at launch.
  • If you hold an AWS WAF private pricing agreement, it stays in force until it expires.
  • The new pricing includes the Security analytics dashboard, which shows full traffic metrics for your protected applications over a rolling 21-day window at no additional cost.

💡 Example: Cost Estimation

Here’s a worked example from the AWS WAF pricing page:

Example 1: One protected resource (Application Load Balancer) serving 20 million requests per month.

  • Resource fee: 1 resource × $0.01 per hour × 730 hours = $7.30
  • Base request fee: 20 million × $0.60 per million = $12.00
  • Total: $19.30 per month

For more pricing details and examples, visit the AWS WAF pricing page. If you have questions about how the new pricing applies to your account, contact your AWS account team or open a Support case.

#AWS #WAF #CloudSecurity #Pricing

Source: Introducing AWS WAF simplified pricing | Amazon Web Services

item.title: CrowdSec provides open-source IDS/IPS and WAF with community blocklists
item.description:
CrowdSec provides open-source IDS/IPS and WAF with community blocklists

CrowdSec is an open-source, participative security solution that offers crowdsourced server detection and protection against malicious IPs. It operates as an all-in-one IDS/IPS and WAF for Linux, Windows, Docker, and Kubernetes environments, allowing users to detect bad behaviors and actively remediate threats through a shared community blocklist.

🔍 Overview

  • CrowdSec is an open-source security solution that is participative by design.
  • It provides IDS/IPS (Intrusion Detection/Prevention System) and WAF (Web Application Firewall) capabilities.
  • It supports Linux, Windows, Docker, and Kubernetes.
  • It features a crowdsourced blocklist of malicious IPs.
  • Detection rules are available under the MIT license.

🧩 How it works

  • Log Analysis: The Security Engine detects bad behaviors by analyzing log sources and HTTP requests.
  • Decoupled Architecture: Following a “Detect Here, Remedy There” approach, users can parse logs on one machine and block threats at a firewall, reverse proxy, or CDN on another.
  • WAF Capabilities: The AppSec component is built on Coraza, allowing SecLang rules and the OWASP Core Rule Set to load as-is. It also supports a YAML rule format.
  • Bot Mitigation: AppSec can answer suspicious requests with a JavaScript proof-of-work challenge at tunable difficulty, stopping headless browsers and scrapers while allowing verified crawlers like Googlebot to pass.
  • Community Blocklist: An IP identified as malicious by one user is added to a curated list, proactively blocking that IP for all other users before it reaches their systems.

⚙️ Key details

  • Scenarios: Ships by default with scenarios for brute force, port scan, and web scan.
  • Customization: Users can extend protection by picking more scenarios from the Hub or creating their own.
  • Remediation: Allows active remediation using Remediation Components.
  • Comparison: Unlike fail2ban, CrowdSec decouples detection and remediation; unlike ModSecurity or naxsi, it shares IP reputation and remediation layers with the log-based engine.

🚀 Availability

  • Installation is available for Linux, Windows, Docker, OpnSense, and Kubernetes.
  • The Community Blocklist is available in real-time.
  • Detection rules are hosted on the CrowdSec Hub.

#CrowdSec #Cybersecurity #IDS #WAF #OpenSource #BotDetection

Source: crowdsecurity/crowdsec

item.title: SafeLine Emerges as Top GitHub Trending WAF Repository
item.description:
SafeLine Emerges as Top GitHub Trending WAF Repository

SafeLine has newly appeared as a top-ranked GitHub trending repository for Go projects, establishing itself as a self-hosted Web Application Firewall (WAF) designed to protect web applications from attacks and exploits.

🔍 Overview

SafeLine is a self-hosted Web Application Firewall (WAF) to protect web apps from attacks and exploits. A web application firewall helps protect web apps by filtering and monitoring HTTP traffic between a web application and the Internet.

🧩 How it Works

Unlike a proxy server that protects a client machine’s identity, a WAF operates as a reverse-proxy, shielding the server by routing client requests through the firewall before reaching the server. A WAF protects web apps by filtering, monitoring, and blocking malicious HTTP/S traffic while preventing unauthorized data from leaving the application. This is achieved through policies that distinguish between malicious and safe traffic.

⚙️ Key Details

SafeLine’s core capabilities include:

Capability Description
Block Web Attacks Defends against SQL injection, XSS, code injection, os command injection, CRLF injection, XXE, SSRF, path traversal, and other web attacks
Rate Limiting Thwarts DoS attacks, bruteforce attempts, traffic surges, and abuse by throttling excessive traffic
Anti-Bot Challenge Blocks bots and crawlers while allowing human users through challenge mechanisms
Authentication Challenge Requires password entry for visitors when enabled, blocking unauthenticated access
Dynamic Protection Dynamically encrypts HTML and JavaScript code with each visit to the web server

Additional features include defenses for web attacks, proactive bot abuse defense, HTML & JS code encryption, IP-based rate limiting, and Web Access Control List.

🚀 Availability

SafeLine has achieved significant recognition on GitHub:

  • #1 GitHub Trending Repository
  • #1 Go Repository of the Day
  • #1 Go Repository of the Week
  • #9 Go Repository of the Month

💡 Why It Matters

The rise of SafeLine highlights growing community interest in self-hosted, open-source security solutions for web application protection, offering organizations an auditable alternative to commercial WAF offerings.

#WAF #cybersecurity #GoLang #GitHub #WebSecurity

Source: chaitin/SafeLine

item.title: AWS WAF Introduces New Security Analytics Dashboard
item.description:
AWS WAF Introduces New Security Analytics Dashboard

AWS has introduced a new security analytics dashboard for AWS WAF, providing a single global page to investigate traffic across all protection packs (web ACLs), Regional resources, and Amazon CloudFront distributions. This update builds on the 2024 traffic overview dashboard by offering a consolidated view that helps users act on findings faster.

🔍 Overview

The new dashboard is designed to help users investigate and contain threats faster while reducing false positives that block real customers. Key aspects of the update include:

  • A single global page for investigating traffic across all protection packs (web ACLs).
  • Coverage of Regional resources and Amazon CloudFront distributions.
  • No need to build or maintain a custom log analytics pipeline.
  • Built on full-fidelity request data rather than samples.
  • Two primary use cases demonstrated: investigating a traffic spike and tuning rules to reduce false positives.

🧩 How It Works

To access the dashboard, users navigate to the AWS WAF console and select “Security analytics” in the navigation pane. The interface allows users to narrow the view to specific protection packs and set time ranges.

  • Global View: The dashboard displays request data across all protection packs in the account. Selecting “All protection packs” shows a comprehensive view.
  • Traffic Breakdown: The top of the page shows total requests split by action: Allow, Block, CAPTCHA, and Challenge.
  • Charts and Widgets: The “Requests chart” visualizes traffic changes over time, while widgets below display top values for specific dimensions. Users can split the Requests chart by dimensions such as Host, Rule triggered, Country, or JA4.
  • Host Grouping: Grouping or filtering by Host identifies which domains are under attack or experiencing spikes, even when a single protection pack protects multiple domains or a domain spans several protection packs.
  • Labels and Detections: AWS Managed Rules add labels (e.g., Bot Control categories, verification status, and signals like non_browser_user_agent). Users can also create custom labels. Because labels are recorded even when a rule is set to count-only, filtering by a label shows what a rule detected across all protection packs without changing how traffic is handled.
  • Filters and Actions: Filters apply to the entire dashboard, updating the action split, Requests chart, widgets, and request list. Users can select any value in a widget to focus on it, remove it, or block it.
  • Request Details: For individual requests, the dashboard displays HTTP fields such as host, path, headers, user agent, and JA4 fingerprint. It also shows which detections and labels matched and whether each action was enforced or only counted.

⚙️ Key Details

Previously, accessing this level of detail required working from a limited sample of requests or setting up and querying custom AWS WAF logs. The new dashboard makes this data available directly. Additionally, the current dashboard view is saved in the user’s browser.

💡 Why It Matters

This tool allows security teams to move from reactive log analysis to proactive investigation and containment. By providing full-fidelity data without the overhead of maintaining custom pipelines, organizations can more effectively tune their rules to minimize false positives and protect their infrastructure.

#AWS #WAF #WebSecurity #CloudSecurity #DataAnalytics

Source: Introducing the new AWS WAF security analytics dashboard | Amazon Web Services
